newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries stay firm in London, awaiting CPI.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries stay firm in London, awaiting CPI.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries in London clung to firm levels on Tuesday, awaiting key inflation data later to provide ammunition for the uptrend, traders said.

Economists said the U.S. May consumer price data due at 1230 GMT could be slightly stronger than last week's producer prices which fell 0.3 percent. Those numbers fuelled expectations that the Federal Reserve will not tighten credit in July.
"It won't be as good as the PPI numbers," said Julian Jessop, economist at Nikko Europe in London.
"But even so the consumer spending is pretty soft at the moment, so you wouldn't expect a nasty surprise either."
By 1000 GMT, the 30-year U.S. bond was quoted at 99-01, yielding 6.70 percent, unchanged from Tokyo and slightly down from New York's close of 99-03.

The consensus forecast for the CPI is a rise of 0.2 percent headline and underlying, against a 0.1 percent headline rise in April. Economists said a rise of 0.5 percent would be considered a "bad number".
Nick Benton, trader at BankAmerica in London, said business was sluggish in London ahead of the CPI. But he noted continued interest from Europe even though single currency worries were dissipating.
"Why would anyone do anything ahead of CPI? The risk is that we will get a bad number one day and the market will not like it," Benton said.
"If you get a good inflation number it's more of the same and the market will push up a little bit more."
Jessop said more than half of the consumer price index consisted of the service sector which isn't taken into account in PPI. A tight labour market would be more evident in the CPI.
But even with a shock CPI, the balance of data was still favourable for the Federal Reserve, Jessop said.
"The motto for today is buy on dips, and that would include any dips after a disappointingly stong CPI," he added.
But comments by the Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin on Monday indicated the Fed was in the dark still.
Rivlin said the economy was slowing down from its exuberant first quarter pace but faced the risk of inflation down the road, and the interest rate decision in July was still a "tough call".
Traders and economists expected the U.S. curve to flatten out further with demand shifting to the 10- and 30-year sector where more gains were on the cards.
Tuesday's economic data includes May industrial production at 1315 GMT and housing starts at 1230 GMT.
September T-bond futures were quoted 2/32 down at 112-00 in automated trade.
